rounds.response:
1. Executive objective recap (1–2 short paragraphs): 1.1 Restatement: Build an AI-assisted requirements-summarization feature embedded in our enterprise project-management platform to convert long requirement documents into concise, actionable summaries (TL;DR, acceptance criteria, and suggested linked tickets) to speed stakeholder alignment and decision-making; assumption: the "PM requirements interviews – key themes (v1)" file is representative of user needs. 1.2 Primary stakeholders: Product Managers; Project Leads; Business Analysts; Engineering Managers; QA Leads.  
2. Current state of our product and users (2–4 paragraphs): 2.1 Our platform currently supports requirements capture via rich-text pages, attachments, linked tickets, version history, commenting, search and tagging but lacks built-in semantic summarization or structured extraction (assumption: feature parity with common PM platforms). 2.2 From the PM interviews, users today manually skim long docs, create offline TL;DRs, assign review tasks, or copy extracts into tickets; pain points include time-consuming manual synthesis, missed or inconsistent requirements, difficulty tracing changes across versions, and friction keeping summaries up to date.  
3. Competitive and benchmark scan (table + commentary) 3.1 Table: Tool / Provider | Primary use case | Type of AI assistance | Notable strengths | Notable limitations; Notion AI | Note-taking & docs | Summarization, rewrite, extraction | Fast inline summaries, integrated editor | Limited enterprise governance and privacy controls; Google Docs (Workspace) | Collaborative documents | Auto-summaries, outlines, smart chips | Ubiquity, good collaboration UX | Generic summaries, limited domain tuning; Microsoft 365 Copilot | Office productivity (Word/Teams) | Contextual summarization, action-item extraction | Deep Office integration, enterprise controls | Cost, data residency complexity; Atlassian Confluence + AI apps | Team documentation / knowledge base | Add-on summarization and page digests | Close to developer workflows, Jira links | Plugin variability and inconsistent UX. 3.2 Commentary: Market patterns show in-editor, fast summarization and basic action-item extraction but limited capability for domain-specific requirement semantics, traceability to tickets/tests, and enterprise governance; this gap aligns with our platform opportunity to deliver structured acceptance-criteria extraction, provenance, and ticket linkage.  
4. Technical feasibility assessment (3–5 paragraphs) 4.1 Approaches: (a) Call a cloud-hosted instruction-tuned LLM via API for on-demand summarization and extraction (fast to prototype); (b) Use embeddings + Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over indexed historical requirements and tickets for domain-aware, provenance-backed summaries; (c) Offer a hybrid private-hosted or customer-managed inference option for sensitive customers; integration points: editor inline summary, a sidebar/summary microservice, backend ticket-linking APIs, and search/index pipelines. 4.2 Key dependencies and integration risks: needs access to anonymized historical requirement docs for prompt engineering or fine-tuning (assumption: we can obtain samples), reliable document chunking and embeddings, budget for inference and storage, latency SLAs for inline vs full-doc summaries (target <3s for snippets, <30s for full-doc), robust RBAC/data-residency controls, and mapping between freeform docs and structured ticket schemas—risks include model hallucination, API throttling, and complexity syncing summaries with version history.  
5. Risk and constraint analysis (bulletized) 5.1 Product / user-experience risks: - Inaccurate or overconfident summaries that omit critical acceptance criteria; - Users over-relying on AI and skipping manual validation; - Workflow disruption or UI clutter if summary placement and update semantics are poor. 5.2 Technical / operational risks: - Data privacy, compliance, and data residency concerns for customer documents; - Model hallucination and ongoing maintenance/finetuning burden; - Latency and cost scaling for large-document processing at enterprise scale.  
6. Preliminary recommendation and next steps (2–3 paragraphs) 6.1 Stance: Pursue — moderate implementation effort with high user ROI given clear pain points and market gaps in domain-aware requirement summarization. 6.2 Three concrete next steps: (1) Prototype (6 weeks) a RAG-based summarization pipeline using an off-the-shelf LLM and 10 anonymized requirement documents to validate accuracy, provenance, and latency; (2) Run 8 usability sessions with PMs, engineers, and QA to validate summary formats (TL;DR, acceptance criteria, linked tickets) and update UX placement; (3) Draft data-governance options and cost/SLA estimates (cloud-hosted vs private inference) to define MLP scope and enterprise offering.

rounds.response:
1. Pilot objectives and hypotheses (1–2 short paragraphs): 1.1 Primary objectives: test whether an AI-assisted requirements-summarization feature reduces the time PMs and teams spend synthesizing long requirement documents, improves the completeness/quality of extracted acceptance criteria, and is acceptable for operational use in our platform (assumption: pilot data and SMEs are available under NDA); 1.2 Hypotheses: H1—AI reduces time-to-decision by ≥25% versus manual synthesis; H2—AI-extracted acceptance criteria achieve ≥85% precision against SME labels; H3—Average user trust/satisfaction ≥4.0/5; (optional H4) AI reduces post-summary change-rate by ≥30%.  
2. Pilot scope and participants (2–3 paragraphs): 2.1 Target roles/segments: Product Managers, Project Leads, Business Analysts, QA Leads, and one engineering liaison per team, across both internal teams and selected customer pilot partners; 2.2 Size/duration: ~8–12 teams total (4–6 internal, 4–6 customers), ~40–120 active users, ~80–200 requirement documents, 6 weeks total (2-week onboarding/baseline + 4-week active test); 2.3 Inclusion/exclusion: include docs >2 pages or >500 words with defined acceptance criteria and teams with weekly cadences and ticket-linking practices; exclude highly regulated documents or customers unwilling to permit pilot data use under NDA (assumption: participating customers will sign pilot agreements).  
3. Metrics, instrumentation, and data collection (table + commentary) 3.1 Table: Metric name | Type | How measured | Why it matters; (1) Time-to-summary | Quantitative | System logs (avg secs per doc) | UX/latency impact; (2) Time-to-decision | Quantitative | Meeting timestamps / user self-report (pre/post) | Productivity/value; (3) Summary accuracy (acceptance criteria precision/recall) | Quantitative | SME annotation vs AI extraction (sampled) | Safety/quality of outputs; (4) Post-summary change-rate | Quantitative | Count of edits/missed reqs within 2 sprints after summary | Indicates omissions/false confidence; (5) User trust & satisfaction | Qualitative | SUS + Likert trust scores + post-task interviews | Adoption and perceived reliability. 3.2 Commentary: these metrics together measure speed (time metrics), output quality and safety (accuracy and post-change rate), and human acceptance (trust/satisfaction); instrument logs, prompt-engineering versioning, and blinded SME annotations are required so we can correlate model outputs with human judgments and usage behavior.  
4. Pilot design and procedures (3–4 paragraphs): 4.1 Key steps: recruit teams and obtain consent/NDAs, run a 1–2 week baseline (manual workflows) collecting metrics, randomize teams to AI-assisted vs control, onboard treatment teams with a short training and in-editor guidance, run 4-week active period collecting automated logs, confidence scores, and sample SME annotations (target ~20% of docs), and conduct weekly 15-minute check-ins plus post-pilot interviews; 4.2 Control/comparison and confound avoidance: randomize at team level (not user level) to avoid cross-contamination, match teams by document complexity and cadence, blind SME annotators to condition when rating accuracy, keep UI/UX identical except for the presence of AI summaries, and ensure dataset sampling for annotation is stratified by document length and type.  
5. Risks, safeguards, and ethics (bulletized): 5.1 Participant/data risks: - Exposure of sensitive or proprietary content during processing; - Hallucinated or incomplete summaries causing downstream errors; - Participant overreliance on AI outputs reducing manual verification; 5.2 Safeguards/mitigations: - Require pilot NDAs, scoped data selection, and opt-in data sharing; - Surface model confidence, provenance links to source text, and require SME sign-off for acceptance criteria before creating tickets; - Provide easy rollback/audit logs, rate-limited edits, and encryption + RBAC for all pilot data; - Log and review any safety incidents immediately and pause feature if high-severity issues arise.  
6. Decision criteria and next-step pathways (2–3 paragraphs): 6.1 Criteria: Success = meet H1 and H2 thresholds (≥25% time reduction AND ≥85% precision) plus average trust ≥4.0/5 and reduced post-summary change-rate ≥30%; Mixed = partial improvements (e.g., time reduced but accuracy between 65–85% or trust 3–4); Failure = no measurable time improvement or accuracy <65% or trust <3 or any safety incidents causing unacceptable risk. 6.2 Next steps per outcome: Success → prepare scale-up plan (phased rollout, SLAs, pricing options, enterprise governance), expand pilot diversity, and start engineering for production-grade integration; Mixed → iterate prompts/UI and run focused A/B tests and model-tuning cycles on problematic doc types for 6–8 weeks, then re-evaluate; Failure → suspend rollout, perform root-cause analysis (data quality, model limitations, UX), consider pivoting to a lower-risk assisted-review feature (e.g., highlighting & sourcing) before reattempting.
